title: UH Mānoa research explores new way to image black holes
excerpt: The study examines how naturally occurring signals from water vapor orbiting black holes could help scientists test fundamental laws of physics.
content:
• November 23, 2026
  • UH News

Reading time: 2 minutes

University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa researchers are exploring a new way to study some of the universe’s most mysterious objects: supermassive black holes.

A new study co-authored by UH Mānoa Department of Physics and Astronomy graduate student Roman N. Burridge and affiliate graduate faculty Geoffrey C. Bower examines how naturally occurring signals from water vapor orbiting black holes could help scientists eventually capture images of their shadows and test fundamental laws of physics.

Published November 6 in The Astrophysical Journal, the research examines 21 galaxies containing water megamasers, powerful natural microwave signals produced by water molecules in gas orbiting supermassive black holes. These signals act as cosmic measuring tools, allowing astronomers to determine a black hole’s mass relative to its distance from Earth and predict how large its shadow should appear.

A black hole’s shadow

A black hole’s shadow is the dark region seen against surrounding glowing material, where light is captured by the black hole’s intense gravity. Imaging these shadows gives scientists a way to study how gravity behaves under extreme conditions.

“Black holes are among the most extreme objects in the universe, and imaging their shadows gives us a way to test how gravity works under those conditions,” Burridge said. “The maser measurements predict the shadow’s apparent size; a future image could test that prediction.”

NGC 4258 has long been a benchmark for studying black holes and measuring cosmic distances. Decades of observations of its orbiting water masers have allowed astronomers to precisely measure its central black hole’s mass and the galaxy’s distance, providing an important reference for measuring distances across the universe.

Building on this research and work by the Megamaser Cosmology Project, the study assesses maser galaxies as targets for future black hole shadow imaging. NGC 4258 stands out: at the observing wavelength considered, it is the only galaxy in the sample whose predicted shadow is large enough to resolve with a telescope on Earth linked to one near the Sun–Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million kilometers away.

However, imaging the black hole’s shadow will require more advanced technology and observations. Researchers also need to determine whether the detected radio emissions originate close enough to the black holes to reveal their shadows. The study provides a foundation for future observations that could expand black hole imaging to more galaxies, helping scientists better understand gravity and the universe.

The Department of Physics and Astronomy is housed in UH Mānoa’s College of Natural Sciences.
